title: Working Within Authorization and Escalation Boundaries

content.overview: Competent technicians know both what they are trained to do and where their authority ends. This lesson teaches routine action, stop-work and escalation boundaries.

vocabulary.definition: Formal permission based on role, training, procedure or assignment to perform a defined action.
Under OSHA lockout/tagout terminology, an employee who operates or uses equipment being serviced or works where covered servicing occurs.
Under OSHA lockout/tagout terminology, an employee authorized to apply energy-control devices for covered servicing or maintenance.

sections.title: Capability is not authorization
sections.body: Recognizing a pesticide restriction, electrical problem, equipment fault or biosecurity hold does not give a technician authority to clear it. Technician I is a routine operational credential, not unrestricted technical authority.

sections.title: Know the maintenance boundary
sections.body: OSHA hazardous-energy rules distinguish affected from authorized employees for covered servicing. When work requires protected access, defeating a guard, opening energized equipment or servicing beyond the assigned operator procedure, the Technician I response is to stop and refer the condition.

workedExamples: A pump alarm may permit a defined external operator check but not opening an electrical panel.
A held room remains restricted until the authorized role clears the hold under procedure.
commonMistakes: Bypassing a guard or control to finish faster.
content.practicalApplication: Classify twelve actions as routine-authorized, stop/hold, maintenance referral, supervisor decision, safety response or emergency response using supplied role rules.
content.summary: Professional performance includes stopping at the correct boundary. Technicians complete authorized routine work and escalate regulated, hazardous, maintenance or supervisory decisions.

blocks.title: Capability, confidence, and authorization are different
blocks.body: A worker may understand a controller, recognize a likely pump problem, know how a guard is removed, or have repaired similar equipment elsewhere. None of those facts alone create current workplace authorization. Technician I performance is defined by the assigned role, training, controlled procedure, and site authority structure.

blocks.alt: Two-sided diagram showing routine operator care such as assigned external inspection, cleaning, setup, visible checks, consumable replacement, and readings on one side, and servicing such as removing guards, entering hazardous motion areas, opening protected electrical components, disassembling powered equipment, or releasing stored energy on the other.
blocks.caption: The boundary is defined by the equipment instructions, site SOP, role, and authorization—not by how easy a repair looks.

blocks.title: Classify the decision before acting
rows: Routine action explicitly assigned in the current SOP
Perform the defined action and record it as required
Unsafe condition outside the routine control
Stop or isolate where authorized and escalate
Equipment fault requiring protected access or covered servicing
Refer to the authorized maintenance/energy-control process
Recognizing the problem does not grant servicing authority
Hold, quarantine, restricted entry, or release decision
Preserve the status and refer to the authorized role
Status clearance belongs to the controlling process
Emergency procedures supersede routine production tasks

blocks.title: OSHA terminology has a specific meaning
blocks.body: Under OSHA's hazardous-energy framework for covered servicing, affected and authorized employees have different roles. A course credential does not by itself make a worker an authorized employee for lockout/tagout or other hazardous-energy servicing.

blocks.title: The controller value is abnormal and the lead is unavailable
blocks.setting: A room value is outside the expected range. The Technician I work instruction tells you to verify the reading and notify the lead, but it does not authorize controller programming. The lead cannot be reached immediately.
options: Change the controller because you understand the setpoint
Keep adjusting until the reading looks normal
Complete the permitted verification, preserve the abnormal status, follow the defined escalation/hold process, and do not expand your authority
Ignore the condition until the lead returns
blocks.answer: Complete the permitted verification, preserve the abnormal status, follow the defined escalation/hold process, and do not expand your authority.
blocks.feedback: The absence of the usual decision-maker does not transfer their authority to the technician. Use the site's alternate escalation or hold process.

blocks.title: Authority-boundary sort
blocks.instructions: Using a supplied role description and SOP excerpts, classify each action into routine-authorized action, stop/hold, maintenance referral, supervisor/quality decision, safety response, or emergency response.
prompts: External pre-use check specified in the equipment SOP
Removing a guard to clear a jam
Verifying an alarm reading without opening protected equipment
Changing a controller program not included in the operator procedure

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Professional competence includes knowing where to stop. Complete assigned routine work confidently, but do not turn knowledge, urgency, or confidence into permission that the role and controlled procedure do not grant.
